headline: Tankers caught fire near Iran again, a reminder that cheaper oil could still flip back up.
summary: Oil averaged $125 a barrel in October, then fell for two weeks as war fears eased. But six tankers caught fire near Iran over the weekend. Gold hit its lowest price in more than a year, because a US rate rise in December now looks nearly certain. Palm oil is piling up in storage for now, even with El Niño on the way.
lookback: The last read came out earlier today, so the monthly price data hasn't changed. Since then, the risk it flagged near Iran showed up: more tankers were hit in the Strait of Hormuz. Gold slipped further, and bets on a December rate rise grew a little. None of the dated things on the watch list has happened yet.

items.title: Tankers burn near Iran, even as oil keeps easing
items.text: Six tankers caught fire near the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday and Monday, CNBC reported. That's the narrow sea lane a lot of the world's oil passes through. Iran's Revolutionary Guards (a branch of its military) said two of them hit mines. Oil had already fallen for two weeks in a row. The US plans to keep its blockade of Iran, which makes big new fighting less likely. The IEA (the world's energy watchdog) expects more oil than buyers need in the last three months of this year. October's average was $125 a barrel, 93% more than a year before. More attacks could push gas prices back up.

items.title: Gold hits its lowest in more than a year
items.text: Gold fell to its lowest price in more than a year on Monday, CNBC reported. It was about $3,880 an ounce, down from a $5,020 average in February. Traders now see a 91% chance that the Fed (the US central bank) raises interest rates in December. Higher rates make gold less attractive, because gold pays no interest. Traders are waiting to hear from the Fed's boss, Kevin Warsh. His words could move gold either way.

items.title: Palm oil piles up for now, before El Niño bites
items.text: Malaysia, a big palm oil grower, had a record amount in storage at the end of October. Its farm board (MPOB) put it at 3.62 million tonnes, the most it has ever held. That is keeping palm oil prices in check for now. Cooking oils overall cost 18% more in October than a year before, by the FAO's count. El Niño (the Pacific running warm) is still getting stronger. Dry weather usually cuts palm harvests many months later. So the squeeze, if it comes, is more likely in 2027 than now.
